# EDSL AgentList

Use `AgentList` to represent respondent personas or other agents in EDSL. Construct from `Agent` instances or use `ep agents create` for CSV and Excel inputs. Keep shared instructions on the list or agents as supported by the current API; represent per-agent differences as traits. See the [construction guide](references/construction.md).

`name` is reserved by `Agent`: pass it as `Agent(name=..., traits={...})`, not inside `traits`. For tabular data, use the `--name-field` option when a column supplies names. Save durable objects with `agent_list.git.save('agents.ep')` and load with `AgentList.git.load(...)`.

Use `ep agents create --help` and `ep agents transform --help` for the installed CLI options. Related EDSL bundles: `edsl:edsl-scenario-lists`, `edsl:edsl-study-files`.

skills.name: edsl-collections
skills.desc: Build, inspect, and publish EDSL Collections that group Expected Parrot objects by typed UUID reference.
skills.body:
---
name: edsl-collections
description: Build, inspect, and publish EDSL Collections that group Expected Parrot objects by typed UUID reference.
tags: [edsl, collections, expected-parrot]
---

# EDSL Collections

Use this skill when someone wants to group, retrieve, or organize EDSL objects with a `Collection`.

A Collection is an ordered, metadata-only list of typed UUID references to objects stored on Expected Parrot. It does not contain member content, freeze a member version, or change member visibility or sharing permissions. Use `ep collections metadata` to resolve current metadata for members the authenticated account can access.

## Create and edit a local collection

Use the installed command help if a CLI option differs by version:

```bash
ep collections create --name "Study materials" --purpose "Survey and prompt for the study." --output study-materials.ep
ep collections add study-materials.ep "$SURVEY_UUID" --type survey
ep collections add study-materials.ep "$PROMPT_UUID" --type prompt
ep collections show study-materials.ep
ep collections metadata study-materials.ep
```

Set `SURVEY_UUID` and `PROMPT_UUID` to UUIDs returned by `ep push`, `ep clone`, or `ep metadata`. Supply each member's type with `--type`. The collection command records references only; it does not fetch member content.

To remove a reference, use `ep collections remove <collection.ep> <uuid> --type <type>`. To build a collection from search, use `ep collections from-search --help`; it creates a collection from one result page. Check pagination data and warnings. Use `ep search` and `ep collections add` to add results from other pages to that collection.

## Publish and retrieve

Collections are `.ep` packages and use the standard object commands:

```bash
ep push study-materials.ep --alias study-materials --description "Survey and prompt references for the study." --visibility private
ep clone "$COLLECTION_UUID" --path study-materials-copy.ep
ep pull study-materials-copy.ep
```

Set `COLLECTION_UUID` to the UUID returned by `ep push`. Collections can also be cloned by owner and alias or by URL.

Visibility applies to the collection object only. A public collection can contain a reference to a private object, but that reference does not grant access to the private object's contents. For visibility, alias, description, and sharing guidance, see `edsl:edsl-object-publishing`.

For the full CLI workflow and search example, see the Collections page in the EDSL documentation.

skills.body:

name: edsl-file-store
description: Use EDSL FileStore and FileStoreList objects for files in scenarios and survey answers.
tags: [edsl, reference]
---

# EDSL FileStore

`FileStore(path=...)` wraps a local image, document, data file, or other supported file for use as an EDSL value. Place it in a `Scenario`, then reference the scenario field in question text, for example `{{ scenario.file_path }}`. EDSL resolves the stored content when constructing the model input.

`FileStore` also provides helpers such as `extract_text()`, `mime_type`, `is_image()`, and `to_scenario_list()` for supported formats. File upload answers can be converted with `FileStore.from_file_upload_answer`; generated image answers can be passed to later image-generation questions. See the [detailed FileStore guide](references/detailed-guide.md).

Related bundles: `edsl:edsl-scenario-lists`, `edsl:edsl-surveys`.

# EDSL human survey agent access

EDSL humanized surveys can expose an agent participation route. Use `ep humanize agent-access get <survey_uuid>` to inspect the configuration and `patch` to update participation mode, general instructions, or question-specific instructions. Consult `ep humanize agent-access --help` for all supported options.

This configuration controls agent access to a human survey. It is distinct from browser respondent links and from the AI chat assistant feature. See the [detailed agent-access guide](references/detailed-guide.md) for modes, config fields, answer limitations, and result representation.

Related bundle: `edsl:edsl-human-survey`.

skills.name: edsl-judgment-evaluations
skills.desc: Design and run EDSL Evaluation workloads for batched, typed model judgments over supplied contexts, then inspect their Results.
skills.body:
---
name: edsl-judgment-evaluations
description: Design and run EDSL Evaluation workloads for batched, typed model judgments over supplied contexts, then inspect their Results.
tags: [edsl, evaluation, typed-judgments]
---

# EDSL judgment evaluations

Use this skill when a task needs a model to classify, choose among explicit
options, assign a binary probability, or score a labeled scale for many
contexts. `Evaluation` batches compatible questions that share a context and
returns the results in EDSL's standard `Results` container. Use regular EDSL
`Jobs` when the task needs generated text, interview execution, branching, or
other normal survey-runner behavior.

## Define and validate the workload

Create a `Survey` with supported typed questions, bind scenarios and an
explicit `JudgmentModel`, then compile before running. Compilation validates
the workload and snapshots it without making inference calls.

```python
from edsl import (
    JudgmentModel,
    QuestionMultipleChoice,
    ScenarioList,
    Survey,
)

survey = Survey([
    QuestionMultipleChoice(
        question_name="sentiment",
        question_text="What sentiment does {{ text }} express?",
        question_options=["positive", "neutral", "negative"],
    ),
])
scenarios = ScenarioList.from_list(
    "text", ["The product is excellent.", "My delivery arrived late."]
)
evaluation = (
    survey.to_evaluation()
    .by(scenarios)
    .by(JudgmentModel("jev-1.13.0", service_name="typesafe"))
)
plan = evaluation.compile()  # No model calls
results = plan.run()         # Requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY
```

Use `await evaluation.run_async()` inside an existing event loop. Bind agents
only when their traits or instructions are part of the judgment context.

Before execution, confirm that the intended behavior fits the supported
semantics:

- Supported questions are multiple choice, yes/no, and linear scale. Linear
  scales need a descriptive label for every level.
- Free-text questions, answer piping, skip/stop rules, survey memory, option
  randomization/pinning, custom question templates, and dynamic or direct-answer
  agents are rejected during compilation. Do not silently approximate these
  features; use a regular EDSL job when they are required.
- Model bindings are explicit. Scenarios and agents combine with models as a
  cross-product; multiple models each evaluate the workload.
- Only visible agent traits are included in the judgment state. Scenario fields
  are sent as context, so avoid putting secrets in scenarios.

The built-in TypeSafe provider reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the process
environment at execution time. Keep credentials out of evaluation definitions
and serialized packages.

## Run, inspect, and recover

Use the normal `Results` analysis methods for answers and metadata. The default
answer is the modal option; `distribution.*` contains the probability vector in
the rendered option order. `resolution_*` fields record any configured
probabilistic resolution. Provider output, model version, and batch membership
are retained in `raw_model_response`.

```python
results = evaluation.run(max_concurrency=8, max_questions_per_request=20)
answers = results.select("answer.*", "distribution.*")
```

If a run raises `EvaluationRunError`, inspect `error.partial_results`. It
contains completed rows and the cache entries for validated batches. Re-run
with that cache to retry incomplete work. Save the cache separately when it
must be reused across processes; a Results package does not retain the
execution cache or per-run cache-used flags.

Save an evaluation definition with `evaluation.save("evaluation.ep")` and
restore it with `Evaluation.load(...)`. Results also support their regular EDSL
serialization. Evaluation definitions can be serialized, but this feature
does not submit work to Coopr: calls go directly from the executing Python
process to the configured judgment provider.

skills.name: edsl-object-publishing
skills.desc: Persist EDSL objects and use the EDSL CLI to push, inspect, share, update, and pull remote objects.
skills.body:
---
name: edsl-object-publishing
description: Persist EDSL objects and use the EDSL CLI to push, inspect, share, update, and pull remote objects.
tags: [edsl, reference]
---

# EDSL object publishing and sharing

EDSL objects persist locally through their `.git.save(...)` interface. The CLI manages remote object lifecycle: `ep push` uploads an object, `ep metadata` inspects it, `ep update-metadata` changes metadata, `ep share` and `ep unshare` manage user access, and `ep pull` retrieves updates. Use `ep <command> --help` for exact flags and `ep auth status` to inspect authentication state.

`ep push` accepts an alias, description, and visibility. Visibility values are `private`, `unlisted`, and `public`; their effects are returned in command metadata. Pushing is a remote write. See [remote object commands](references/remote-object-commands.md) for common operations. This bundle documents the EDSL interface and object model; approval procedures and publishing decisions are EP Agent workflow policy.

Use installed CLI help for command details.

# EDSL remote object search

Use `ep search --query <text> --page 1 --page_size 50` to search available objects. Inspect metadata and object type, then use `ep clone <owner>/<alias> --path object.ep` or `ep pull object.ep` as appropriate. `ep inspect` and `ep metadata` expose local package details. # EDSL respondent orchestration

Use `edsl.workflows` when a study is a durable graph of respondent work: who
gets each step, when it becomes ready, which earlier answers it can observe,
and how completion or retries release later work. This is the respondent
orchestration API; `ep workflow` is a separate CLI for research-task evidence
gates.

Start with `Workflow` to author steps and dependencies. Use conditions, quorum
completion, derived values, and bounded repeats only when the protocol requires
them. Route participants with an `ExecutionPlan` to `human`, `llm`, or
`scripted` executors. Use shared state when transitions need durable common
state across interviews; see `edsl-shared-state` for its Machine and scope
contracts.

For portable bundles, use `WorkflowExperiment` to combine the compiled workflow,
state maps, participants, and executor plan. Validate and inspect the serialized
bundle before execution. Choose `ep orchestration run` for scripted/LLM runs or
answer replay. Choose `start`/`sync`/`status` for Humanize delivery. Read
[CLI lifecycle details](references/cli-lifecycle.md) before starting a run,
especially when model calls or participant invitations are involved.

The API and serialized format are experimental and versioned. Preserve the
experiment definition, output directory, and instance ID when resuming. Use the
same replay answer file on every replay-driven resume. Read
[workflow authoring and execution](references/authoring-and-execution.md) for
the object model and durable-run invariants.

Fetch complete, version-matched workflow examples through the CLI with
`ep skills show edsl-orchestration --example <path>`. Use
`ep skills list --routing` to find available examples, or see the
[example guide](references/examples.md). The Humanize delivery example requires
two explicit email addresses before it can create a run or send invitations.

skills.name: edsl-results-validation
skills.desc: Compare simulated EDSL survey results with human responses. Check survey compatibility, choose population or record-level comparisons, and create a reproducible study-specific analysis script with clear uncertainty and limitations.
skills.body:
---
name: edsl-results-validation
description: Compare simulated EDSL survey results with human responses. Check survey compatibility, choose population or record-level comparisons, and create a reproducible study-specific analysis script with clear uncertainty and limitations.
tags: [edsl, results, human-data, validation, analysis]
---

# Compare simulated results with human responses

Use this skill when a user wants to understand whether simulated respondents
answer like real respondents, or wants to compare model-generated answers with
human judgments. The first task is to identify what kind of comparison their
study supports. Do not assume every human-versus-simulation comparison is the
same problem.

## Choose the estimand before writing code

There are two distinct goals:

- **Population-level response patterns:** compare answer distributions between
  the simulated sample and human sample. This is appropriate when there is no
  one-to-one correct human answer for each simulated respondent. Use marginal
  distributions overall or within comparable subgroups.
- **Record-level agreement:** compare predictions and human labels for the same
  underlying records, cases, or vignettes. This requires a stable shared record
  identifier and a defensible human reference label. Do not describe a marginal
  distribution comparison as record-level accuracy.

Ask one concise question if the user's goal or the shared unit is unclear. If
there are multiple human judgments per record, preserve them for an inter-rater
analysis or document how adjudicated labels were made; do not silently select
the first response or treat an unresolved majority as ground truth.

## Inspect inputs and check comparability

Read the project files and inspect both `Results` objects before choosing
columns or metrics. Use `ep inspect <file.ep>` for local packages and the
available `Results` APIs for loaded objects. Humanize results can be retrieved
with `Coop().get_human_survey_responses(uuid)` when the user supplies or has
already authorized use of the survey UUID. Do not publish data, submit a job,
or contact respondents as part of this analysis.

Before calculating a comparison, make a compact compatibility table for every
question being considered:

| Check | What to verify |
|---|---|
| Identity | Both datasets contain the same intended item; matching names alone are not proof. |
| Type and scale | Question types, option labels, value coding, and scale direction agree. |
| Wording and conditions | Question wording, instructions, question order, and relevant scenario text are equivalent. |
| Routing and missingness | Skips, nonresponse, failed answers, and partial submissions have the same inclusion meaning. |
| Sampling unit | Identify a human respondent, simulated agent, scenario/record, model, and iteration; determine which rows are independent. |
| Subgroups and weights | Verify variables have the same definitions and coding on both sides; inspect missing and invalid weights. |

Stop or narrow the analysis when a material mismatch remains. Explain the
mismatch and either harmonize it with a documented rule, compare only the
compatible questions, or ask the user how to proceed. Never silently equate
different labels or reverse-coded scales.

## Build a study-specific analysis

This capability is an analysis workflow, not a built-in `ResultsFidelity`
method. Create a small, readable Python script in the study's existing analysis
directory (or ask where to save it if there is no clear location). The script
should load the user's existing result artifacts, perform the checks above,
calculate the selected comparison, and save machine-readable tables plus a
short interpretation. Do not rerun model jobs or collect human responses to
complete the comparison unless the user asks.

Prefer the smallest set of methods that answer the research question:

- **Nominal, single-choice answers:** show option shares side by side and a
  per-option difference. Total variation distance (TVD) is a useful compact
  summary: half the sum of absolute share differences, bounded from 0 (same
  shares) to 1 (no overlap). Jensen-Shannon distance is another bounded summary
  when a symmetric information-based measure is useful. Include the option
  table so the summary is interpretable.
- **Ordinal scales:** report the full category distribution and an ordinal
  summary such as mean/median or cumulative-share differences. Treating ordered
  categories as nominal may discard useful information; explain the metric if
  using TVD or Jensen-Shannon distance.
- **Numeric responses:** inspect range, units, and shape; compare meaningful
  summaries or distributions. Bin only with substantively justified cut points
  and report them.
- **Checkbox / multi-select answers:** compare selection rates separately for
  each option. These are not a single-choice distribution and their shares need
  not sum to one.
- **Free text:** use a documented coding rubric or a separate evaluation
  instrument. Do not compare raw string equality as if it measured semantic
  agreement.
- **Same records with reference labels:** join by the stable record identifier,
  validate join cardinality, report unmatched rows, then use a task-appropriate
  agreement measure. Keep human disagreement visible when there is no adjudicated
  reference.

Subgroup comparisons are useful only when the subgroup has the same meaning on
both sides and enough observations to interpret. Always report unweighted row
counts for each side and group. If using survey weights, validate finite,
non-negative values, explain the weighting target, and distinguish respondent
counts from weighted shares. Report effective sample size when weights vary
substantially.

## Uncertainty and dependence

Use uncertainty estimates only after identifying the sampling unit and design.
For independent respondent samples, a respondent-level bootstrap can show how
sample variation affects the distance. For repeated observations of the same
person, multiple iterations of an agent, clustered scenario assignment, or
repeated model runs, resample at the independent cluster (or use a suitable
design-based method); row-wise resampling would understate uncertainty.

A nonnegative distance has finite-sample upward bias, so a percentile bootstrap
interval can remain above zero even when samples come from the same population.
Do not interpret “interval excludes zero” as a test that the distributions
differ. If useful, compute a human split-half reference by repeatedly dividing
the human respondents into two groups and comparing their distributions. Label
it as a descriptive sampling-noise reference, not a significance threshold or
formal pass/fail criterion. State that half-samples are smaller than the full
human sample and therefore generally have more sampling variation.

Report methodological choices alongside results: included questions, exclusions,
missing-answer rule, weight variable, subgroup definitions, resampling unit,
metric, random seed, and number of resamples. Do not claim representativeness or
population validity from a convenience sample or a distance score alone.

## Deliverables

Create a reproducible analysis script and save outputs beside it, typically:

- a question compatibility table;
- a per-question (and per-model/subgroup, when relevant) summary table;
- option-level shares and differences;
- optional uncertainty estimates with the sampling unit stated;
- a concise Markdown interpretation noting limitations and unresolved mismatches.

Keep outputs traceable to source result files and avoid overwriting existing
reports. Before finishing, summarize which comparison was performed, what was
excluded, where the script and outputs were saved, and what the results can and
cannot establish.

## Related EDSL workflows

Use `edsl:edsl-human-survey` for deploying and retrieving human surveys, and
`edsl:edsl-prolific` when the user wants a paid, screened sample.

---
name: edsl-scenario-lists
description: Construct EDSL ScenarioLists from Python data, files, combinations, images, or other supported sources.
tags: [edsl, reference]
---

# EDSL ScenarioList

Use `ScenarioList` to represent scenario variations for surveys and jobs. Construct from `Scenario` instances, dictionaries, supported CSV/Excel inputs, or combinations. For image scenarios, use `Scenario.from_image(...)` and reference the image field in every question that needs the image.

A scenario value must be used in question text where required by EDSL jobs compatibility checks. `ScenarioList` supports normal mutable-sequence operations, including `.append()`. Save durable artifacts with `.git.save(...)`.

skills.name: edsl-shared-state
skills.desc: Design, validate, run, and inspect EDSL shared-state machines for durable state shared across interviews. Use when responses update common state, adaptive mechanisms, quotas, or scoped group state are required.
skills.body:
---
name: edsl-shared-state
description: Design, validate, run, and inspect EDSL shared-state machines for durable state shared across interviews. Use when responses update common state, adaptive mechanisms, quotas, or scoped group state are required.
tags: [edsl, shared-state, state-machine]
---

# EDSL shared state

Use shared state when multiple interviews need to read or update durable, typed
state through explicit transitions. Keep the machine definition, its scope, and
its storage backend conceptually separate:

- `Machine` defines fields, commands, requirements, views, and completion rules.
- `SharedState` groups named machines into one state space.
- `SharedStateMap` selects a separate state space for each scope key.
- A runner or workflow backend persists state as the work executes.

Start from the invariant the mechanism needs to enforce, then express it in a
machine. Machine definitions are serializable data; do not put Python callbacks
or model calls inside a machine. Validate definitions and capability requirements
before executing them. See [machine design and scopes](references/machines-and-scopes.md).

For survey integration, attach state reads, questions, and writes in execution
order. Use typed answer references such as `question.answer`, not strings that
look like Python expressions. Pick a stable scope key for the participants who
share state, and reuse the same serialized state map when resuming a run. See
[survey execution and state provenance](references/survey-execution.md).

Fetch complete, version-matched source examples through the CLI with
`ep skills show edsl-shared-state --example <path>`. Use
`ep skills list --routing` to find example paths, or see the
[example guide](references/examples.md).

The `ep` CLI can validate, inspect, and locally simulate serialized Machine JSON,
then inspect shared-state bindings in saved Results. It does not author a full
Machine interactively or persist the `state simulate` dry run. See
[shared-state CLI commands](references/cli.md).

This feature is experimental and versioned. Prefer the installed EDSL package's
schemas, CLI help, and matching references over examples from another release.
For multi-step assignment, branching, Humanize delivery, or respondent-level
workflow recovery, use `edsl-orchestration`; a workflow may use shared state as
one of its coordination mechanisms.

---

---

# EDSL study files

Keep object construction in readable source files, export named EDSL objects, and save durable objects with their supported `.git.save(...)` interface. Build `Jobs` from the saved component objects with `ep jobs build`; run it with `ep run ... --output results.ep`. Do not run inference as an import-time side effect of a Python source file.

Use `ep inspect agents.ep --markdown --page 1 --page-size 5` to present a page of agents with stacked traits and instructions. The same command previews saved scenarios, models, jobs, results, surveys, collections, and prompts. Check the exit code before presenting the Markdown.

Common files include `study_survey.py`, `study_scenario_list.py`, `study_agent_list.py`, and optionally `study_model_list.py`. Use `ep models create` for ordinary model selections when it covers the needed configuration.

Use the installed CLI help and `edsl:edsl-surveys` for current APIs. A scenario field must be consumed by the survey where required by the installed EDSL validation rules. `Agent.name` is a distinct constructor field, not a trait.

This skill covers EDSL file and object conventions only. Study design choices, cost approval, remote execution policies, reporting workflows, and EP Agent scaffolds belong to the separately managed EP Agent environment (`ep-agent:workflow-file-layout`, `ep-agent:workflow-model-selection`).

# EDSL cost tools

Use `ep jobs cost jobs.ep` to estimate a saved job and `ep results cost results.ep` to inspect actual costs. Estimates depend on model pricing, prompt size, iteration counts, token overrides, and skip logic; consult [estimation details](references/estimation-details.md) and [calibration and branching](references/calibration-and-branching.md) for calculation details.

Use `ep balance` to inspect the configured account balance and `ep balance alert` to manage low-balance notifications. Cost estimates and alerts are EDSL features; study budget approval and whether to run a job are separate workflow decisions.

# Build an EDSL survey

Use this skill for EDSL API questions about survey construction and for implementing survey objects. Check installed-version help and schemas when CLI details may differ.

EDSL questions are stateless by default. When a later question depends on an earlier choice, pipe each relevant answer into its question text with `{{ question_name.answer }}` or use an appropriate memory mode. Do not add unrelated prior answers.

To present a saved survey in a terminal, run `ep surveys show survey.ep --markdown`. Add `--with-question-names` or `--with-question-types` to label the headings. Add `--expand-options` to list every dropdown choice. On success, stdout is Markdown you can include directly in your reply. Use `ep surveys show survey.ep` for the JSON summary.

For detailed API behavior, use [survey reference](references/survey-reference.md), [full reference](references/full-reference.md), [composition contracts](references/composition-contracts.md), and [probabilistic responses](references/probabilistic-responses.md).

Related EDSL guidance: `edsl:edsl-quirks` and `edsl:edsl-study-files`.

Optional EP Agent cross-references may appear as `ep-agent:<skill-name>`. They describe research workflows or platform processes and are not part of the EDSL API.
